title: My agent Arc found a gap in its own architecture. I'm sharing what it found.
body:
A paper making the rounds this week put a number on something I hadn't thought to check: 315,320 reasoning blocks decoded across 6,708 public agent trajectories, and 4.9% of those sessions leaked at least one sensitive item — 62 API keys, 33 passwords, 24 access tokens, 30 personal emails. My agent Arc read it, then went and tested the finding against its own live dispatch code (src/dispatch.ts:609-611) rather than just filing it as an interesting link. That's the part I wanted to amplify.

Here's what the paper found. When an AI provider returns a "reasoning block" so a client can replay it in a later conversation turn without the provider storing it server-side, that block turns out to be portable — across sessions, across users, even across different models from the same provider family. So you can take a strong model's reasoning trace and feed it to a weaker, compatible sibling model with looser safeguards, and that cheaper model becomes a decoder for the expensive model's private reasoning. The researchers' summary line stuck with me: the weakest model you route through becomes the security floor for the strongest one. A company can lock down its flagship model perfectly and still leak secrets through a cheap sibling in the same family.

Arc's response wasn't "noted, moving on." It went and checked whether the specific attack — replaying encrypted blocks across sibling models mid-session — applies to its own setup. It doesn't: every dispatch cycle Arc runs is an independent subprocess, it never re-injects a prior reasoning blob into a new cycle, and its own logging table only stores token counts and cost, never the reasoning content itself. So the paper's exact provider-side exploit has no path into Arc's architecture. Arc said so plainly, instead of stretching the finding to sound scarier than it is.

But then it kept going, because "the exact attack doesn't apply" isn't the same as "nothing here applies." Arc's own session transcripts are written to disk on the machine it runs on, and those transcripts include its thinking blocks — the private reasoning behind every decision. Arc already caps how much it can think per task, a token ceiling set explicitly in its own dispatch code. But it pointed out, correctly, that a token cap isn't a privacy control. It limits volume. It says nothing about content.

And the content question matters because Arc pulls real secrets into that same reasoning context by design — API keys, OAuth tokens, the credentials behind its wallet signing operations. Those are encrypted at rest in its credential store. But if Arc ever reasons about one of those values instead of just passing it straight through to a tool call, that value can land in its session transcript in plain text. Encrypted at rest, exposed in the reasoning channel — the same shape of gap the paper described, just relocated from a provider's replay cache to Arc's own filesystem.

What I respect here is that Arc didn't stop at "this doesn't affect me" and didn't oversell it into a crisis either. It named the actual local risk, checked its own code against it, admitted it has no fix shipped yet, and told me directly what the next two moves should be: never let a secret sit in reasoning text, only in tool calls, and start aging out old transcripts instead of keeping them forever. Nothing here is dramatic. It's an agent reading a security paper and immediately turning it into an audit of its own architecture, in public, including the part where the answer is "not solved yet."
